issues.legal_issue: A surety is not discharged under the rule concerning loss of security when the security becomes unavailable through operation of law rather than an act attributable to the creditor.
material_facts: The borrower created mortgages and other security for loans, and personal guarantees were given for repayment.
Legislation nationalised the borrower’s undertakings and vested their assets in the State, making the original security unavailable to the creditor.
The creditor’s loss of the original security was not caused by a deliberate act of the creditor.
issues.conclusion: The sureties were not discharged on account of the loss of the security, because that loss resulted from operation of law and was not attributable to an act of the creditor.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 139 and 141 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a surety may be discharged where the creditor acts inconsistently with the surety’s rights or loses or parts with security through an act attributable to the creditor; Section 141 does not discharge the surety for a fortuitous loss beyond the creditor’s control. The Court relied on State of Madhya Pradesh v. Kaluram, State Bank of Saurashtra v. Chitranjan Rangnath Raja, China and South Sea Bank Ltd. v. Tan, and the principle stated in Rees v. Barrington.

rule.if: surety_guarantee_claim and security_unavailable_by_operation_of_law and not creditor_caused_security_loss

predicates.surety_guarantee_claim: A creditor seeks to enforce a guarantee against a surety for a borrower’s debt.
predicates.security_unavailable_by_operation_of_law: The creditor’s security becomes unavailable because a legal change transfers or affects the secured assets.
predicates.creditor_caused_security_loss: The creditor acts or omits to act in a way that causes the security to be lost or impaired.

issues.definition: When a creditor seeks payment from a surety and the security became unavailable by operation of law rather than through an act of the creditor, the surety is not discharged for that loss.

issues.legal_issue: Nationalisation of a borrower’s undertaking does not extinguish the borrower’s prior liability or the surety’s independent liability under a guarantee.
material_facts: The borrower owed amounts under loans and related facilities, and guarantors had undertaken joint and several liability for repayment.
The nationalisation legislation vested the borrower’s undertaking and assets in the State and provided for claims against the undertaking to be dealt with through compensation.
The legislation preserved the borrower’s liability for prior obligations, and the guarantee documents required payment upon default.
issues.conclusion: The borrower’s liability and the guarantors’ liability continued after nationalisation; the legislation changed the mode of recovery against the secured assets but did not extinguish the guarantee.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 3, 4, 5 and 20 of the Sick Textile Undertakings (Nationalisation) Act, 1974, read together, did not extinguish the owner’s prior liabilities or the guarantor’s liability. Section 128 of the Indian Contract Act makes the surety’s liability co-extensive with the principal debtor’s unless the contract provides otherwise. The Court relied on Maharashtra State Electricity Board v. Official Liquidator and Punjab National Bank v. State of U.P.; it also noted the principle in Patheja Bros. Forging & Stamping v. ICICI Ltd. that clear statutory language must be given effect.

predicates.nationalisation_debt_recovery_claim: A creditor seeks recovery of a debt connected with an undertaking that has been nationalised.
predicates.prior_borrower_debt_exists: The borrower incurred the debt before the undertaking was nationalised, and the debt remains unpaid.
predicates.guarantee_secures_that_debt: A surety gave a guarantee covering repayment of the borrower’s debt.

issues.definition: Where a creditor seeks a debt incurred before nationalisation and a guarantee covers that debt, nationalisation does not extinguish the borrower’s or surety’s liability.

issues.legal_issue: A guarantee is not frustrated merely because a supervening event changes the borrower’s circumstances or the creditor’s means of recovering security, where payment under the guarantee remains possible.
material_facts: The borrower defaulted on its repayment obligations and the guarantee was invoked for the unpaid amount.
Nationalisation affected the assets securing the debt, but did not make payment under the guarantee impossible.
The guarantors also relied on the ending of the borrower’s managing-agency arrangement, but that change did not make performance of the guarantee impossible.
issues.conclusion: The doctrine of frustration did not apply, and the guarantors remained bound to honour the guarantee.
issues.legal_principle: Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, applies where a contractual obligation becomes impossible of performance after contracting, not merely where performance or recovery becomes more difficult. The Court relied on F.A. Tamplin Steamship Co. Ltd. v. Anglo-Mexican Petroleum Products Co. Ltd., Naihati Jute Mills v. Khyaliram, and Davis Contractors v. Fareham U.D.C. It treated the guarantee as an independent contract that remained performable despite the supervening events.

predicates.guarantee_enforcement_proceeding: A creditor brings proceedings to enforce a guarantee after the borrower defaults.
predicates.payment_under_guarantee_is_due: The borrower has failed to pay an amount covered by the guarantee, triggering the guarantor’s payment obligation.
predicates.supervening_event_does_not_make_payment_: A later event changes the borrower’s circumstances or the creditor’s recovery options but does not make payment under the guarantee impossible.

issues.definition: If a creditor seeks payment under a guarantee that has been triggered and a later event does not make payment impossible, the guarantee is not frustrated.

issues.legal_issue: A creditor may pursue a civil suit while also claiming payment through the statutory compensation process, but cannot recover the same amount twice.
material_facts: The creditor filed a civil suit for the unpaid debt and also lodged its claim with the Commissioner of Payments under the nationalisation legislation.
The Commissioner allowed a substantial part of the creditor’s claim, leaving a balance that remained the subject of the suit.
issues.conclusion: The statutory claim did not bar the civil suit, but any amount received through the Commissioner had to be credited against recovery in the suit.
issues.legal_principle: The nationalisation legislation did not, on the Court’s reading, take away a claimant’s right to pursue both the statutory compensation process and a civil suit, subject to preventing double recovery. The Court agreed with Oriental Coal Co. Ltd. v. Mohanlal Kisanlal and Barakar Coal Co. Ltd. v. N.C. Mehta.

predicates.civil_debt_suit: A creditor brings a civil suit to recover an unpaid debt.
predicates.statutory_compensation_claim_for_same_de: The creditor also claims through a statutory process for compensation relating to the same debt.
predicates.payment_received_through_compensation_pr: The creditor receives some payment through the statutory compensation process.

issues.definition: When a creditor sues for a debt and also claims statutory compensation for it, the suit may proceed, with payments already received credited against recovery.
